questions.stem:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
At time $t=0$, a particle $P$ is at the fixed point $O$
At time $t$ seconds, $t>0$, $P$ has position vector $\mathbf{r}$ metres relative to $O$, where
$\mathbf{r}=\left(3t+2-2\sqrt{t+1}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(t^2-6t\right)\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the speed of $P$ at the instant when $P$ is moving in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{i}$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Use $\mathbf{v}=\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt}$. Differentiate the vector. At least 3 powers going down.
A1: $\mathbf{v}=\left(3-(t+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\mathbf{i}+(2t-6)\mathbf{j}$ one component correct
A1: both components correct.
M1: $(2t-6)=0\Rightarrow t=3$ Equate their $\mathbf{j}$ component of velocity to zero and solve for $t$. Must have seen a clear attempt to differentiate.
A1: Speed $=2.5(\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1})$ or equivalent. Must be a scalar. A0 for $2.5\mathbf{i}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ when $t=0.25$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Use $\mathbf{a}=\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}$. Differentiate the vector. Powers going down and at least one constant goes to zero.
A1: $\mathbf{a}=\frac{1}{2}(t+1)^{-\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ or equivalent correct expression. Allow if correct derivative implied by correct substitution.
DM1: $\left(\mathbf{a}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{125}}\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}\right)$, $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{\frac{16}{125}+2^2}$ Correct use of Pythagoras. Dependent on the preceding M1.
A1: $=2.03(\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2})$ or better ($\frac{2\sqrt{645}}{25}$ or 2.0317...)

parts.label: c
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: For $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0}$, $\left(3t+2-2\sqrt{t+1}\right)=0$ and $\left(t^2-6t\right)=0$. No need to consider $t=0$ as this is excluded in the Q.
A1: $t\neq0\Rightarrow t=6$ but $\left(3\times6+2-2\sqrt{6+1}\right)\neq0$. Hence no solution and does not return. Clear explanation of the given result with no errors seen, e.g. $\left(3t+2-2\sqrt{t+1}\right)=0 \Rightarrow 9t^2+8t=0$ has no solution for $t>0$ (need something to indicate impossible).
Note: There will be other alternatives, e.g. show that the horizontal component of the velocity is always $>2$, so no return. M1 for correct strategy A1 for correct conclusion with no errors seen and sufficient justification. Conclusion needs to be clear but does not need to be the exact wording from the question. An argument dependent solely on acceleration is unlikely to work.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- An argument dependent solely on acceleration is unlikely to work – do send to review if you find one worthy of merit.

questions.stem:
[In this question $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are unit vectors, with $\mathbf{i}$ horizontal and $\mathbf{j}$ vertically upwards.]
Figure 3 shows a diagram (not to scale) of the motion of a particle $P$.
The fixed points $A$ and $C$ lie on horizontal ground.
The point $B$ is vertically above $A$, with $AB=10\,\mathrm{m}$.
At time $t=0$, a particle $P$ is projected from $B$ with velocity $(x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, where $x$ and $y$ are positive.
Particle $P$ moves freely under gravity and hits the ground at $C$.
At the instant before $P$ hits the ground, the velocity of $P$ is $(3\mathbf{i}-15\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, as shown in Figure 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $x=3$ seen or implied anywhere. Do not accept $x=3\mathbf{i}$.
M1: Use of $v^2=u^2+2as$ Complete method using suvat or energy to form an equation in $y$. Condone sign errors.
A1: $15^2=y^2+2\times g\times10$ Correct unsimplified equation.
A1: $y^2=29$, $y=5.4$ or $5.39$ 2 sf or 3 sf. If final answer is $y=5.4\mathbf{j}$ do not penalise inclusion of a vector a second time.
Alt (Energy): B1: $x=3$ seen or implied anywhere. M1: Equation for conservation of energy require all 3 terms and no extras, dimensionally correct, must include $m$: $\frac{1}{2}m\left(3^2+15^2\right)=mg\times10+\frac{1}{2}m\left(x^2+y^2\right)$. A1: correct unsimplified equation - any equivalent form. A1: $y^2=29$, $y=5.4$ or $5.39$. SC allow 4/4 for $x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}=3\mathbf{i}+5.4\mathbf{j}$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- NB: For the whole of this question, confusion between horizontal and vertical is not a misread

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Time from B to C: Complete method using suvat and their vertical speed. Condone sign errors.
A1ft: $-15=5.39-gt$ ($t=2.08$) Correct equation in $t$ only, e.g. $10=15t-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$. ft on their 5.39 if used.
DM1: Horizontal distance $=3t$ ($=$ their $x\times$ their $t$) Complete method using suvat and their $x$ value. Dependent on preceding M1.
A1: $(AC=)6.2(\mathrm{m})$ or $6.24(\mathrm{m})$ 2 sf or 3 sf. NB Penalise over-accuracy only once per question.

questions.stem:
A uniform rod $AB$ has length $8a$ and weight $12W$.
The end $A$ of the rod is freely hinged to a fixed point on a vertical wall.
The rod lies in a vertical plane that is perpendicular to the wall.
A particle of weight $W$ is attached to the rod at $B$.
A light inextensible string of length $5a$ has one end attached to the rod at the point $C$, where $AC=5a$.
The other end of the string is attached to the wall at the point $D$, where $D$ is above $A$ and $AD=8a$.
Angle $DAC=$ Angle $ADC=\theta$, as shown in Figure 6.
The rod and the particle rest in equilibrium.
The tension in the string is $T$.

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) NB: This is a "show that" question. The working must give a clear indication of where the lengths in the moments equation come from. Check the diagram. Could be resolving or using similar triangles. Might have resorted to using a calculator to evaluate the angles. Each term should include a trig ratio.
M1: Moments about A. Or an alternative complete method to form an equation in $T$. Condone sign errors and sine/cosine confusion. Need all terms and dimensionally consistent (accept with no $a$).
A1: $12W\times4a\sin\theta+W\times8a\sin\theta=5a\times T\sin2\theta$ or $48aW\sin\theta+8aW\sin\theta=8aT\sin\theta$ Unsimplified equation with at most one error.
A1: $48aW\sin\theta+8aW\sin\theta=3aT\cos\theta+4aT\sin\theta$ or $\left(48\times\frac{3}{5}W+8\times\frac{3}{5}W=T\times10\times\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{4}{5}\right)$ Correct unsimplified equation. Allow A1A0 if angle DCB used and not in terms of $\theta$. If no trig in the moments equation then M0 – given answer, so no BOD.
A1*: $56W=8T\Rightarrow T=7W$ Obtain given answer from correct working.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) The force exerted on the rod by the hinge at $A$ acts at $\alpha°$ above the rod, where $0<\alpha<90$
Find the value of $\alpha$.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: First equation e.g. resolve horizontally. Condone sign errors and sine/cosine confusion.
A1: $(\pm)H=T\sin\theta\left(=\frac{21}{5}W\right)$ Correct unsimplified equation. Alt: resolving parallel to the rod: $13W\cos\theta=T\cos2\theta+R\cos\alpha$.
M1: Second equation e.g. resolve vertically. Condone sign errors and sine/cosine confusion.
A1: $(\pm)V+T\cos\theta=13W\left(V=\frac{37}{5}W\right)$ Correct unsimplified equation. Alt resolving perpendicular to the rod: $13W\sin\theta=R\sin\alpha+T\sin2\theta$.
Another alternative is to use a second moments equation e.g. M(C): $5a\times R\sin\alpha+W\times3a\sin\theta=12W\times a\sin\theta$; M(B): $R\sin\alpha\times8a+T\sin2\theta\times3a=12W\times4a\sin\theta$
DM1: $\alpha°=\tan^{-1}\frac{3}{4}-\tan^{-1}\frac{H}{V}$ or $\tan^{-1}\frac{V}{H}-\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3}$ Complete method to obtain $\alpha$. Dependent on the two preceding M marks. Alt gives $R\sin\alpha=\frac{27}{25}W$, $R\cos\alpha=\frac{211}{25}W$.
A1: $\alpha=7.3$ 7.29205... or better. Mark 0.127 radians as a misread.
